<!-- Generated by `node scripts/docs-reference.mjs`. Do not edit. -->

Normalize measures the loudest peak in the selection and scales everything so that peak lands exactly where you ask. It is the usual last step before export: the file uses its full range without ever clipping. It also removes any DC offset, the slight vertical shift some sound cards add.

:::note[Coming from Audacity?]
This is Audacity's **Effect → Volume and Compression → Normalize**. The names below are Soundscaper's own, which sometimes differ.
:::

## Steps

1. Open Soundscaper. A new, empty project is ready as soon as the editor loads.
2. Choose **File → Import audio** and pick your recording. This lesson uses `lesson-quiet-take.wav`. The file lands as a clip on its own track.
3. Choose **Select → Select all**.
4. Choose **Effect → Volume and compression → Normalize**. In the **Normalize** dialog, set **Peak amplitude** to `-3`, then press **Apply to selection**. Minus three decibels leaves a little headroom for the encoder if you export to MP3 later.
5. Press **Play** to listen, then **Stop**.
   *You should see:* The loudest moment now sits just under full scale.

## Tips

- Normalize looks at peaks, not at how loud the recording feels. Two normalized files can still sound very different; for that, see [Normalize loudness for a podcast](/lessons/normalize-loudness-for-podcasts/).
- Stereo channels are normalized together unless you turn on **Normalize stereo channels independently**, which can shift the stereo image.

## About this lesson

Every step on this page is replayed against each build of Soundscaper by the browser suite (`tests/browser/soundscaper-lessons.spec.js`). If a menu entry, field or button stops matching, the build fails until the lesson is corrected, so the steps you read are the steps the editor accepts.
